Q: SwiftUI layout differ based on view you have? A:

There are two main issues here:

Why Color yellow does not fill all screen?

This is because the yellow color in InnerView is being applied as background to Text. A background view, like an overlay, adopts the frame of the view it is applied to. So the frame of the view is being determined by the Text.

The other questions concern safe area edges and boil down to the following: when are safe area edges ignored?

The safe area edges are only ignored if:

  1. a view is actually in contact with the safe area edges, and
  2. the safe area edges are explicitly ignored.

Why blue go out of border? Why Blue fill safe area?

The blue color ignores the safe area edges because it is in contact with the edge of the safe area (point 1 above) and safe area edges are being ignored explicitly (point 2).

The reason why safe area edges are being ignored explicitly is because you are applying the background as a ShapeStyle using background(_:ignoresSafeAreaEdges:):

.background(Color.blue)

The default value for the parameter ignoresSafeAreaEdges is .all. If you don't want to ignore the safe area edges, then you can either supply an empty set of edges instead:

.background(Color.blue, ignoresSafeAreaEdges: [])

or... you you use curly braces instead of round parentheses. This then goes to background(alignment:content:):

.background { Color.blue }

Regarding the second code example:

Why then ColorView make background yellow beyond safearea when colors itself not?

The colors red and green are not ignoring safe area edges. If you want them to, try applying .ignoresSafeArea(), for example:

Color.red
    .ignoresSafeArea()

The yellow background does ignore the safe area edges, for the same reason as explained above.

Q: What is the struct tag of anonymous structs in C? A:

it's not specified, but you can assume that is some random name that you don't have access to. This makes every anonymous struct impossible to reuse (except if you have aliased it with a typedef) and different to any other.

Q: How do I create a dictionary of dictionaries in Python? A:
  • No need to read the whole file into memory
  • Use batched
  • A list seems more appropriate than dict (like I wrote), then you don't need to track the number manually
from itertools import batched

entries = []
with f:
    for name, line1, line2 in batched(f, 3, strict=True):
        entry = {
            "Name": name.strip(),
            "Line1": line1.strip(),
            "Line2": line2.strip()}
        entries.append(entry)

(assuming entry and Sat in your code are empty dicts)

or as a list comprehension:

from itertools import batched

with f:
    entries = [
        {"Name": name.strip(), "Line1": line1.strip(), "Line2": line2.strip()}
        for name, line1, line2 in batched(f, 3, strict=True)
    ]

Q: Can terraform resource arguments be used as attributes? A:

In the Terraform plugin protocol, which OpenTofu also currently relies on, each resource type has a single schema that describes both what is valid in configuration and what is included in an object representation of an instance of that resource type.

Generally-speaking, any attribute that's usable as a configuration argument is also exposed as an attribute of an object representing a resulting resource instance. And Terraform and OpenTofu both impose a set of rules on providers about how the resulting object must match the configuration.

To summarize those rules a little, the following details are relevant to this question:

  • For any attribute that can be used as a configuration argument, the provider is required to either return exactly the configured value or exactly the value that was returned the previous time changes were applied to that object.

    Providers return the previous value in situations where the currently-configured value is semantically equivalent to the previous value, such as if an argument accepts JSON syntax and only the insignificant whitespace has changed, or if a string is interpreted as case-insensitive by the underlying API and only the case of letters has changed. This exception avoids annoying situations where meaningless cosmetic changes would otherwise cascade down to any other resources whose configuration refers to the value that has changed.

  • The provider is allowed to choose its own value for any attribute that is left unspecified (or, equivalently, set to null) in the configuration.

    This is how providers implement "default values", for example: you leave the argument unset in the configuration, and then the provider returns its chosen default value as part of its response to Terraform's request for a plan.

  • In any case where the provider is allowed to choose a value itself as in the previous point, the provider is allowed to report during the planning phase that it doesn't yet know what the final value will be.

    Terraform and OpenTofu both report this in their plan UI as (known after apply). If you use such a value as part of an expression elsewhere in the configuration then the result of that expression will typically also be "known after apply", because Terraform/OpenTofu cannot fully evaluate that expression until the inputs become known during the apply phase.

One notable exception to this rule is the recently-added concept of "write-only attributes" for managed resources. A provider is allowed to declare an attribute as being "write-only" and in that case that attribute always appears as null when referred to from elsewhere in the configuration. This is designed for situations where the underlying API accepts an argument as input but provides no way to read back the previously-chosen value for that argument, such as when accepting passwords and other secret values.

Any reference to any part of a resource in the configuration for another resource causes an implicit dependency between the resources. It does not matter which specific attributes you refer to. Using depends_on with a resource address that already appears in at least one expression elsewhere in the same resource configuration is always redundant.
